implementation_notes: Rust enums are sum types in the language: `enum Payment { Card { number: String }, Transfer { iban: String } }` fixes the variant set, each variant carries exactly its own fields, and `match` is checked for exhaustiveness, so adding a variant breaks every non-exhaustive match at compile time - a hard error, not a lint. Values are immutable unless a binding is explicitly `mut`, `#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]` supplies the case-class conveniences (copying stays explicit), and recursive variants need indirection (`Box`, `Rc`). `#[non_exhaustive]` is the deliberate escape hatch that lets a library grow its variant set without a breaking change, at the cost of forcing downstream wildcard arms. Use the sealed-trait variant instead when the closed set is a set of separate types rather than cases of one value.
pitfalls: `#[non_exhaustive]` trades closure for compatibility: downstream matches must keep a wildcard arm, so the compiler can no longer point at every site a new variant must be handled.

Matching a borrowed enum (`p: &Payment`) binds fields by reference (`number: &String`), so anything needed as owned data must be cloned explicitly; writing the match as if it owned the value fails to compile.
The enum is as large as its biggest variant because payloads are inlined, not boxed - relevant when a small variant is stored in bulk; box the heavy payload or split the type.
`mut` is per binding, not per type: an owned enum in a mutable variable can still be mutated through `&mut`, so shared values should be exposed as `&` or behind `Arc`.

variants.name: Sealed trait (private supertrait) with visitor or downcast
variants.idiom_name: pub trait X: private::Sealed + visitor/downcast elimination
variants.implementation_notes: When the design must stay trait-driven - variants are separate types plugged into existing bounds, or dispatch should be monomorphized - the closure is expressed with a sealed trait: a public trait whose supertrait lives in a private module (`pub trait Payment: private::Sealed`), so the unnameable `Sealed` bound means only this crate can implement it (Rust API guidelines, C-SEALED). Case analysis is then a visitor method or downcasting through `Any`, and totality is not checked the way `match` is, so the crate must keep the implementor list and its matchers in sync. Prefer this form for closed sets of behaviours or implementations, and for the semver freedom it buys (adding methods to a sealed trait is not a breaking change); prefer the enum when the cases are values.
pitfalls: Sealing is invisible to callers and to rustdoc: downstream users see an implementable-looking trait, so the seal must be documented explicitly (the API guidelines require it).
Downcast-based elimination fails at run time when a variant is missed, whereas `match` fails at compile time - the sealed trait is the weaker closure for case analysis.
Sealing prevents downstream implementations but not method-call breakage: adding methods is safe, removing or changing a public method signature is still breaking.
